questions.prompt: In a conflict, what appears between ======= and >>>>>>>?

options.text: The 'ours' side (your current branch in a merge)

questions.explanation: The text from ======= to >>>>>>> is the 'theirs' side — the incoming branch in a merge, or your replayed commit during a rebase.

options.text: Records your conflict resolutions and replays them when the same conflict recurs

questions.explanation: rerere ('reuse recorded resolution') remembers how you resolved a conflict and reapplies that resolution automatically the next time the identical conflict appears.

questions.prompt: Which statements about resolving conflicts are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: git status lists conflicted files under 'Unmerged paths'
After resolving a file, you git add it
git merge --abort cancels a conflicted merge
It's fine to commit a file that still has conflict markers

questions.explanation: status shows unmerged paths, you stage resolved files with git add, and --abort cancels. Committing leftover markers ships broken content — always remove them.

questions.prompt: After resolving all conflicts during a rebase, proceed with: git rebase --________
questions.explanation: git rebase --continue resumes the rebase after you've staged the resolved files (or git rebase --abort cancels it).

questions.prompt: During a REBASE, which side does `<<<<<<< HEAD` refer to?

options.text: The branch you're rebasing onto (the base)

questions.explanation: During a rebase, Git replays your commits onto the target, so HEAD (ours) is the base branch and 'theirs' is your commit — the reverse of a merge. Mixing this up leads to discarding the wrong side.

questions.prompt: Match each command/idea to its effect.

pairs.right: Take your side of a file

questions.explanation: --abort cancels, --continue resumes, --ours takes your side, and rerere replays a past resolution.
